overview: This 1,045-page file documents the reconstruction, regulation, and expansion of Japan’s radio system under the Allied occupation from 1946 to 1949. It combines institutional material on the Broadcasting Corporation of Japan with SCAP directives, State Department correspondence, diplomatic exchanges, and exceptionally detailed registers of broadcasting, land, maritime, police, aeronautical, meteorological, railway, and international radio stations. Much of the file traces changing licenses, frequencies, call signs, equipment, locations, operators, and service restrictions, while smaller policy files address international broadcasting, ship-to-shore service, frequency planning, the Ryukyu Islands, and interference involving stations in Europe and North Korea.
interest: The file is especially useful because it joins high-level occupation policy to a remarkably granular technical map of Japan’s postwar communications network, including individual vessels, police installations, international circuits, and station coordinates. Its successive registers and amendments permit historians to reconstruct how radio infrastructure changed over time and to study the relationship between communications control, maritime activity, policing, civil aviation, and state reconstruction. The correspondence on revived international broadcasting, suspicious inquiries about Kyodo, mistaken identification of interference, and the Hamhung dispute also reveals how technical radio problems became matters of intelligence, diplomacy, and early Cold War politics.
